title: Maths reference: Number
summary: The words and methods from Number Foundations, each with an example and, where it helps, a picture of the number line.
_about: Maths cards for maths/number (see snippets/maths.json for the format).

items.label: integer
items.hint: A whole number, zero, or a negative whole number.

items.label: negative number
items.hint: A number below zero, to the left of $0$ on a number line: five below zero.

items.label: less than, greater than
items.hint: The wide end of the sign faces the greater number. Further left on the line is less.
items.board:
widget: numberline
range: -10, 10
point A: -7
point B: -2
compare: A, B
items.shows: −7 is further left than −2, so −7 < −2

items.label: further from zero
items.hint: The size of a number without its sign. Among negatives, the one further from zero is the lesser: $-10 < -1$.

items.label: square number
items.hint: A number times itself: the area of a square with that side. The perfect squares to 144: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100, 121, 144.
items.board:
widget: square
s: 6
items.shows: A 6 by 6 square covers 36 unit squares

items.label: square root
items.hint: The number that times itself makes this one: the side of a square with that area. Not half: $\sqrt{36} \ne 18$.

items.label: base and exponent
items.hint: The base (2) is multiplied; the exponent (5) counts how many times. $2^5$ is not $2 \times 5$.

items.label: prime
items.hint: A number with exactly two factors, 1 and itself. 1 is not prime.

items.label: mixed numeral
items.hint: A whole number and a fraction. A negative one is both parts below zero: one and a half below zero.

items.label: power of 10
items.hint: Each place value column is a power of 10. The exponent counts the zeros, and the ones column is $10^0 = 1$.

items.label: expanded notation
items.hint: A number as the sum of each digit times its place value. A column holding 0 adds nothing, so leave it out.
items.board:
widget: placevalue
places: 5
n: 4052
items.shows: 4052 on the columns: 4 × 10³ + 5 × 10¹ + 2 × 10⁰

items.label: decimal places
items.hint: The number of digits after the decimal point. To 2 decimal places means to the nearest hundredth.

items.label: estimate
items.hint: A quick, close answer from rounded numbers. Round to the first digit and keep the size; then compare with the exact answer.
items.board:
widget: rounding
mode: estimate
a: 38
b: 52
op: ×
items.shows: 38 × 52 ≈ 40 × 50 = 2000; the exact answer is 1976

items.label: ratio
items.hint: Compares quantities in a stated order. The first thing named is the first number.
items.board:
widget: ratio
mode: tape
labels: red, blue
a: 2
b: 3
items.shows: 2 red blocks to 3 blue blocks

items.label: part to part, part to whole
items.hint: Part to whole adds the parts: $2 + 3 = 5$. The part-to-whole ratio $2 : 5$ matches the fraction $\tfrac{2}{5}$.

items.label: equivalent ratios
items.hint: Multiply or divide both terms by the same number. Adding the same number to both changes the ratio.
items.board:
widget: ratio
mode: tape
labels: flour, milk
a: 2
b: 3
k: 3
items.shows: Three copies of 2 : 3 make 6 : 9

items.label: simplest form of a ratio
items.hint: Divide both terms by their highest common factor (here 6). No number above 1 divides both.

items.label: scale
items.hint: A ratio of the drawing (or model) to the real thing. Each 1 unit on the drawing is 50 units in real life.

items.label: known, unknown, relationship
items.hint: The first step in modelling: say what you know, what you need, and how they are linked. Then calculate.

items.label: percentage change multiplier
items.hint: One change after another: multiply the multipliers. Up 20% then down 20% is × 0.96.
items.board:
widget: money
mode: change
q: 100
a: 20
b: -20
units: $
items.shows: $100 up 20%, then down 20%: $96

items.label: tax brackets
items.code: \text{each part of the income} \times \text{its bracket's rate}
items.hint: The marginal rate is the rate on the last dollar; the effective rate is total tax ÷ income.

items.label: rate
items.hint: A rate compares quantities with different units (km per h, $ per kg); a ratio compares the same kind. 1 km/h = 1000 m ÷ 3600 s: divide by 3.6 for m/s.
items.board:
widget: rate
top: km, distance
bottom: h, time
rate: 60
x: 2.5
items.shows: At 60 km per hour, 2.5 hours matches 150 km

items.label: using a rate
items.hint: Write the units in: km ÷ km/h = h. Then check the size makes sense.

items.label: model assumptions
items.hint: Every model assumes something (steady speed, no fees, no starting charge). When it disagrees with real life, name the assumption and refine the model.

items.label: adding a negative
items.hint: Start at the first number. Adding a positive moves right; adding a negative moves left.
items.board:
widget: numberline
range: -10, 10
sum: a + b
slider a: -10, 10, 4
slider b: -10, 10, -6
items.shows: From 4, left 6, to −2

items.label: subtracting
items.hint: Subtracting moves the opposite way to adding: subtracting a positive moves left, past zero if it has to.

items.label: subtracting a negative
items.hint: Adding $-3$ would move left 3, so subtracting it moves right 3. It gives the same as adding $3$.
items.board:
widget: numberline
range: -10, 10
sum: a - b
slider a: -10, 10, 5
slider b: -10, 10, -3
items.shows: Adding −3 would go left; subtracting it goes right 3, to 8

items.label: multiplying integers
items.hint: Same signs give a positive, different signs a negative. On the line: $a$ jumps of $b$; a negative number of jumps goes the opposite way.
items.board:
widget: numberline
range: -12, 12
labels: 2
product: a × b
slider a: -4, 4, -3
slider b: -4, 4, -2
items.shows: −3 jumps of −2 go the opposite way: to 6

items.label: dividing integers
items.hint: The same sign rule as multiplying, because dividing undoes it: check $3 \times (-4) = -12$.

items.label: between two squares
items.hint: Find the perfect squares either side and take their roots. Square decimals to get closer: $6.6^2 = 43.56$, so $\sqrt{43} \approx 6.6$.
items.board:
widget: square
s: 6.6
target: 43
items.shows: A square of side 6.6 is just over the dashed target of 43

items.label: prime factorisation
items.hint: Split into factor pairs until every branch is a prime, then write repeated primes with exponents. Every tree gives the same primes.
items.board:
widget: factortree
number: 60
grown: on
items.shows: A factor tree for 60 ending in the primes 2, 2, 3 and 5

items.label: HCF and LCM
items.hint: HCF: the primes both share. LCM: all the primes, shared ones once. Sharing into equal groups needs the HCF; things lining up again need the LCM.

items.label: equivalent fractions
items.hint: Multiply (or divide) the top and the bottom by the same number: the same amount, cut into more (or fewer) parts. Adding the same number to both changes the amount.
items.board:
widget: bars
a: 2
b: 3
c: 8
d: 12
items.shows: 2/3 and 8/12 shade the same amount

items.label: simplest form
items.hint: Divide the top and the bottom by their highest common factor. In simplest form (lowest terms) they share no factor but 1.

items.label: fraction to percentage
items.hint: Percent means out of 100: make the fraction out of 100, or work out the decimal and multiply by 100.
items.board:
widget: bars
a: 3
b: 4
c: 75
hundred: on
show: decimal, percent
items.shows: 3/4 of the bar is 75 of 100 squares

items.label: fraction to decimal
items.hint: Divide the top by the bottom. Some never end: $\tfrac{1}{3} = 0.333\ldots$

items.label: decimal and percentage
items.hint: Decimal to percentage: × 100 (0.5 is 50 hundredths, not 5%). Percentage to decimal: ÷ 100.

items.label: percentage to fraction
items.hint: Put it over 100, then simplify.

items.label: adding fractions
items.hint: Cut both into the same parts first (a common denominator; the LCM is the lowest), then add the tops. Never add the bottoms.
items.board:
widget: fracadd
a: 1
b: 3
c: 1
d: 4
k: 12
items.shows: Thirds and quarters both cut into twelfths: 4 + 3 = 7 twelfths

items.label: multiplying fractions
items.hint: Multiply the tops and the bottoms, then simplify. Multiplying by a fraction less than 1 makes smaller.
items.board:
widget: fracarea
a: 2
b: 3
c: 3
d: 4
items.shows: 3/4 of 2/3 of a square: 6 of 12 parts

items.label: dividing by a fraction
items.hint: How many fit? Dividing by a fraction is multiplying by it flipped (top and bottom swapped): $\tfrac{2}{3} \div \tfrac{1}{6} = \tfrac{2}{3} \times 6 = 4$.

items.label: percentage of an amount
items.hint: Of means multiply. Mentally: 10% is a tenth (8), 5% is half of that (4).
items.board:
widget: percent
q: 80
p: 15
items.shows: 15% of a bar of 80 is 12

items.label: increase and decrease
items.hint: 15% off leaves 85%: × 0.85. 15% on makes 115%: × 1.15. For what percentage, divide and × 100: $18 \div 24 = 75\%$.
items.board:
widget: percent
q: 80
p: 15
mode: decrease
items.shows: 15% off 80 leaves 68

items.label: quick strategies
items.hint: Change the order ($4 \times 2.7 \times 25 = 100 \times 2.7$), change the form (0.75 = 3/4), or split ($12 \times 2.5 = 24 + 6$). Then estimate to check.

items.label: placing a negative fraction
items.hint: Split each unit into equal parts and count from zero. A negative counts left, and the part counts further from zero, not back towards it.
items.board:
widget: numberline
range: -2, 2
fractions: 4
point A: -1.25
point B: -0.75
items.shows: Quarters: A at −1 1/4, B at −3/4

items.label: negative fractions and decimals
items.hint: The integer sign rules hold for every fraction and decimal. Sign first, then size.

items.label: efficient order
items.hint: Multiply in any order, pairing friendly numbers; or split a number: $6 \times (-2.5) = 6 \times (-2) + 6 \times (-0.5)$.

items.label: round to decimal places
items.hint: Look at the digit straight after the place. 5 or more rounds up; 4 or less leaves the digit. Halfway rounds up.
items.board:
widget: rounding
x: 3.746
d: 2
items.shows: 3.746 is past the halfway mark 3.745, so it rounds to 3.75

items.label: estimating
items.hint: Round each number to its first digit, keep its size, calculate, then compare with the exact answer.

items.label: share in a ratio
items.hint: Add the parts, divide the total by the parts to find one part, then multiply. The shares add back to the total.
items.board:
widget: ratio
mode: share
labels: Ana, Ben
a: 2
b: 3
total: 60
units: $
items.shows: $60 in the ratio 2 : 3: five parts of $12, Ana $24 and Ben $36

items.label: profit as a percentage
items.hint: A percentage profit or change is out of the original amount, the cost, not the selling price.

items.label: percentages in two steps
items.hint: Each percentage is of a different amount, so they cannot be added: 20% off then 10% off is not 30% off.
